notes:
I've written notes for every verse except v. 9 and v. 23. A few gaps are worth knowing up front:

- **Some tool results were cut short.** The Enduring Word page stopped partway through v. 14, and Ellicott's Luke 8 page stopped at v. 22.
- **Verses 22–25 (the storm) are thin.** I had very little on them.
- **Some traditions are missing.** I didn't find a Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran or Orthodox reading of these verses, or anything from prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. Those are left out, not guessed.

The Calvinist/Arminian and Protestant/Catholic notes are marked **[Differences]** and **[Other views]** in the verses where they come up.

---

**v. 1**
- Ellicott says the word for "afterward" is the same word Luke used for "in order" in 1:3. Only Luke uses it, and it shows he was still trying to tell events in sequence. The verse sums up a stretch of work that isn't otherwise recorded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik thinks this is often taken as Jesus' *second* tour of Galilee (the first is in 4:42–44). The Twelve were with Him this time; they hadn't yet been formally chosen on the first tour. The good news was that God's Messiah and King was present, announcing His kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/

**v. 2**
- Guzik says Luke names these women because it was unusual. Jesus treated women differently from the religious teachers of His day. He points out that Scripture never says Mary Magdalene was immoral. That idea is a later assumption, and he quotes Leon Morris saying nothing in the sources supports it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- Ellicott says Magdala was a town near Tiberias. The "seven demons" point to an especially severe possession, like that of the Gadarene demoniac. She seems to have been among the wealthier Galileans. He also notes later legends: the Western one has her living as a penitent near Marseilles and Arles, the Eastern one has her dying at Ephesus with the Virgin Mary and John. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott thinks the women may have travelled ahead of the group to arrange food and lodging, a bit like the Shunammite woman who looked after Elisha (2 Kings 4:10). He says it wasn't unusual for women with their own money to support a rabbi. Chuza, as manager of Herod's money, "must have been a man of some mark." Chuza might even be the royal official of John 4:46; if so, Joanna's giving could have come from gratitude for her son's healing. Luke probably knew some of these women personally, as eyewitnesses (Luke 1:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik sees Jesus' humility here: He chose to depend on others' support. He quotes Barclay on how striking it is to find Mary Magdalene, with her dark past, alongside Joanna from the court. He also quotes Pate that the word for their support (*diakonia*) looks ahead to the later office of deacon and deaconess. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/

**v. 4**
- Guzik says "parable" means something "thrown alongside" a truth. A parable usually teaches one main point, and he quotes Barclay warning against turning parables into allegories where every detail means something. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- Ellicott says Luke's setting is less precise than Matthew's, and Jesus may have told the parable more than once. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik says that in that culture seed was scattered first and ploughed in afterward. He prefers to call it the parable of the *soils*: the seed is always the same, and only the ground changes. The path was too hard for anything to grow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- Ellicott says only Luke includes the detail that the seed was "trodden down." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott says only Luke has "because it lacked moisture." In the spiritual meaning, the moisture is the dew and rain of God's grace, without which the seed can't put down roots. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik describes this as a thin layer of soil over a shelf of rock: it warms quickly, so the seed sprouts fast, but it can't root. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/

**v. 7**
- Ellicott says the thorns did their damage by growing *alongside* the good seed until they overpowered it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik says this soil was fertile, perhaps too fertile, because it grew weeds as well as grain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/

**v. 8**
- Ellicott says Luke leaves out the 30/60/100 scale found in Matthew and Mark and mentions only the highest yield. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik reads "He who has ears to hear" as a call for the spiritually sensitive to take special notice, not a general call to everyone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/

**v. 10**
- **"Mystery":**
  - Guzik: in the Bible a mystery is something you'd never know unless God revealed it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
  - Cambridge Bible: in the New Testament the word always means something once hidden and now revealed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm
- **Why Jesus used parables:**
  - Guzik: parables are like doorways or puzzles. Those who were interested could go through. The hardened heard only a story, which spared them the extra guilt of rejecting a plain message. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
  - Pulpit Commentary: Jesus deliberately veiled the truth from careless hearers. It quotes Morrison that the deeper problem is the sinner's own wish not to see, for fear of being won over. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm
  - Godet: the purpose of parables is to veil truth from the indifferent; they attract some and repel others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsc/luke-8.html
- **Gill (Baptist, strongly Calvinist):** spiritual knowledge of the gospel is a "special and peculiar gift of God." Those outside are not "the favourites of heaven." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm
- **A softer reading in the Biblical Illustrator:** one writer there rejects reading the verse as a sentence of permanent ignorance. He takes it as describing people who have hardened themselves and are wilfully ignorant. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/8-10.htm
- **[Modern scholarship]** The Expositor's Greek Testament notes that Luke tones this hard saying down compared with Matthew and Mark, "as if it contained an unwelcome idea." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott says "the word of God" here means every way God reveals Himself to people. It stands in for Matthew's "word of the kingdom." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik says the seed has life in itself, and links this to 1 Peter 1:23. He quotes Spurgeon that the preacher doesn't make the seed; it is given to him by his Master. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/

**v. 12**
- Guzik says Satan is actively at work whenever the word is preached. He is "punctual," knows the power of the word, and really does take the word away. Without the Holy Spirit's opposing work, nothing would happen when the word is preached. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- Ellicott says only Luke uses "the devil" here (Mark has "Satan," Matthew "the wicked one"). Luke also states the devil's purpose more fully: "lest they should believe and be saved." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm

**v. 13**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott: the "time of testing" means tribulation or persecution, as the other Gospels make clear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
  - Guzik: their problem was the lack of moisture, which he takes as the Holy Spirit. He lists Spurgeon's signs of it, such as "faith without repentance" and "zeal without communion." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
  - Pulpit Commentary: these are impulsive people who take up Christ's yoke "with joy, but without thought." https://biblehub.com/luke/8-13.htm
- **[Differences] Was their faith real, and did they lose salvation?**
  - **Reformed (R.C. Sproul):** some read this verse as teaching that saved people can lose salvation. Sproul says that goes against the Bible's teaching on the perseverance of the saints. Believers may backslide seriously but never fall away fully and finally: "If you have it, you never lose it." https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/parable-sower-luk8
  - **Evangelical (bible.org Lesson 34):** this lesson rejects the view that three of the four soils are saved. Believing "for a time" is not saving faith, because the end result is not faith. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-34-superficial-and-genuine-believers-luke-84-15
  - **Matthew Henry:** he calls this hypocrisy that shows itself under trial; they fall away "from their good beginnings." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-13.html
  - **Constable (dispensational):** in a short extract, he says some in Jesus' day "genuinely believed on Him and then stopped believing." This differs from the two views above. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-13.html
  - **Methodist/Wesleyan:** I couldn't read Wesley's own note on this verse, so no Wesleyan view is given here.

**v. 14**
- Ellicott says only Luke adds "pleasures" to the list, and only he has "bring no fruit to perfection." Luke's word for "life" (*bios*) is different from the "world/age" in the other Gospels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- The bible.org lesson gives Judas as an example of someone in whom greed choked the word. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-34-superficial-and-genuine-believers-luke-84-15

**v. 15**
- Ellicott says "noble and good" was a common pairing among Greek moral writers for the highest moral ideal. He prefers "with perseverance" to "with patience": it's an active steadfastness, like "he who endures to the end." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Matthew Henry adds that we are thankful to "free grace" if what is only a puzzle to others is plain truth to us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott says "lamp" and "lampstand" are better translations than "candle" and "candlestick." Mark places this saying in the same spot, which suggests Jesus really said it as part of explaining the sower. Only Luke mentions people "entering" the house. Ellicott wonders whether that reflects Luke's own experience as a Gentile convert who saw the light as he came in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- William Kelly says that once the disciples had been given light, the next step was to give light to others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-10.html

**v. 17**
- Ellicott says this was a saying Jesus used often, in different settings: in the sending of the Twelve (Matthew 10:26), here after the sower, and against hypocrisy in Luke 12:2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Godet sees a deliberate contrast: the light grows in vv. 16–17 while the darkness grows in v. 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsc/luke-8.html

**v. 18**
- Ellicott prefers "what he *thinks* he has." Someone who doesn't use what he knows doesn't really possess it, and he will lose even that. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Matthew Henry says the gifts we have will be kept or lost depending on whether we use them for God's glory and others' good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm

**v. 19**
- Ellicott says this is the same event as in Matthew 12 and Mark 3. Luke puts it after the parables, while the others put it before, and Ellicott thinks the evidence favours their order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- **[Differences/Other views] Who were Jesus' "brothers"?**
  - **Guzik:** Jesus "plainly had many brothers and sisters." He says perpetual virginity goes against the plain meaning of the Bible, and quotes the Catholic scholar Fitzmyer that the New Testament gives no sign of Mary as "ever virgin." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
  - **GotQuestions:** the most natural reading is that they were half-siblings, children of Joseph and Mary. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-siblings.html
  - **Catholic (catholic.com):**
    - Mary never had other children. The "brothers" were either Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage (the usual view before Jerome) or cousins. https://www.catholic.com/tract/brethren-of-the-lord
    - The cousin view rests on Matthew 27:56 and John 19:25, which link James and Joses to another Mary. https://www.catholic.com/qa/how-can-mary-be-a-perpetual-virgin-when-the-bible-says-jesus-had-brothers-and-sisters
  - **NET Bible note:** says the question has a long history in the church. Epiphanius in the 4th century argued Mary was a perpetual virgin with no other children. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Luke+8%3A19-21

**v. 20**
- Ellicott thinks this may be a detail Luke learned from Mark when they met in Rome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm

**v. 21**
- Ellicott says Luke's "word of God" takes the place of "the will of God" in Mark and "the will of my Father" in Matthew. That shows how much the phrase covers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm
- Guzik says we draw close to Jesus by hearing His word and doing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- Matthew Henry says Christ treats faithful hearers who are also doers as His family. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-10.htm

**v. 22**
- Ellicott says Luke's "on one of the days" is vaguer than the time notes in Matthew and Mark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/8.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sees a deliberate pairing: Jesus calms the storm, then the demoniac. Having made peace in nature, He then makes peace in a tormented soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html
- R.C. Sproul (Reformed) says the disciples' question "Who is this?" is answered, with irony, by the demons in v. 28. They knew they were facing God incarnate. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/legion

**v. 26**
- **[Modern scholarship/textual question]** The older manuscripts differ between "Gerasenes," "Gergesenes" and "Gadarenes."
  - The Pulpit Commentary places the event at the ruins of Kerza (Gergesa) and suggests early preachers named the better-known Gerasa or Gadara instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-26.htm
  - The same page reports a note that "Gergesenes" is almost certainly the right reading. It also says Origen knew of a small town called Gergesa. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-26.htm
  - The Homiletical commentary says "Gerasenes" was once rejected because the only Gerasa then known was about fifty miles away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html
- Ellicott says Luke explains where the region was ("opposite Galilee"), the way a foreigner writing for foreigners would. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-26.htm
- Constable says the region was mostly Gentile, so Luke may have seen this as a preview of the church's mission to the Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html

**v. 27**
- Precept Austin says living among the tombs was considered a sign of madness, and unclean spirits were thought to rule over the dead. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- Barclay says, whatever we think of demons, they were intensely real to the people of Gerasa and to this man, who was violently insane. He notes Jesus' courage in facing him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html
- Coffman disagrees with explaining it away: what happened "was real." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html

**v. 28**
- **What the demons knew about Jesus:**
  - Constable: the demons recognised Jesus as God. They weren't worshipping Him; they were appealing to their judge for mercy and wanted to escape being tormented in the abyss early. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html
  - MacArthur (gty.org): the demon panicked in the presence of "his executioner." The demons' "theology is orthodox": they knew who Jesus was when some disciples weren't sure. He links the title to Luke 1:32. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-109/the-maniac-who-became-a-missionary-part-1
  - Hiebert (quoted by Precept Austin): Luke's verb for "fell down" doesn't necessarily mean worship. Hiebert calls it a forced confession of who Jesus is. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62156/
- **About the title "Son of the Most High God":**
  - Homiletical commentary: the title appears only here, in Luke 1:32, and in Acts 16:17 (another possessed person). The man's identity is so confused that sometimes he speaks and sometimes the demons do. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html
  - Pulpit Commentary: the title may have been commonly used in exorcisms. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html
  - Adam Clarke: several manuscripts leave out "Jesus" and "God," and he thinks the demons may have avoided saying those names. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html
- **"Torture":** Precept Austin says the Greek verb (*basanizō*) means severe torment or distress. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- **Application:** The Biblical Illustrator says Christ didn't come to torment people. He came to save them from the sins and demons that are their real tormentors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-28.html
